name: Chang'an
subtitle: Daxing, the Tang Capital, and Ming Xi'an
description: Chang'an from the Sui foundation of Daxing in 582 to the Ming walled city of Xi'an: the Palace and Imperial Cities, the Daming Palace on its plateau, the two markets and the walled wards of the northern and central city down to the Greater Wild Goose Pagoda. The far western, southern and south-eastern wards lie beyond the frame. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Yong'an canal
water.blurb: Dug in 582 to bring water of the Jiao river north through the western wards, past the West Market and out under the north wall into the Forbidden Park. Its exact line through the wards is the usual reconstruction.

water.name: Qingming canal
water.blurb: A Sui canal from the Jue river, led north through the wards west of Zhuque Avenue into the Imperial City and on to the pools of the palace gardens.

water.name: Longshou canal
water.blurb: The 'Dragon Head' canal, dug in 583 from the Chan river east of the city, entering by the Tonghua gate and running west to the Palace City; a branch fed the Xingqing pond.

water.name: Longshou canal (Xingqing branch)
water.blurb: The branch that fed the Dragon Pond of the Xingqing Palace.

water.name: Longshou canal
water.blurb: Restored in the early Ming to bring Chan river water through the east wall to the city and the moat of the Prince of Qin's palace; the city's wells were brackish.

water.name: City moat
water.blurb: The moat round the Ming walls, fed by the canals; drawbridges crossed it in front of the four gates.

hills.name: Longshou plateau
hills.blurb: The 'Dragon Head' plateau, a loess ridge north of the city. Its southern tip carried the Daming Palace, whose Hanyuan Hall stood some 15 m above the wards; the Tang could look down on the whole city from it.

hills.name: Leyou plateau
hills.blurb: The highest ground inside the walls, in the south-east wards, a park and picnic place where people climbed on the ninth day of the ninth month. Li Shangyin's quatrain on it ends: 'The setting sun is infinitely lovely, only the dusk is near.'

hills.name: Leyou plateau
hills.blurb: The old pleasure ground of the Tang, now fields and the ruins of the Qinglong temple, where the Japanese monk Kūkai had studied esoteric Buddhism in 805.

roads.name: Zhuque Avenue
roads.blurb: The Avenue of the Vermilion Bird, 150 m wide from ditch to ditch, from the Imperial City's Zhuque gate 5 km to the Mingde gate. No house opened onto it: only the walls and gates of the wards, locust trees and drainage ditches. It divided the city into the eastern Wannian and western Chang'an counties.

roads.name: Chengtianmen Street
roads.blurb: The axis through the Imperial City from the Zhuque gate to the Chengtian gate, lined with the offices of government.

roads.name: Hengjie (the Transverse Street)
roads.blurb: A square-cum-street some 220 m wide between the Palace City's south wall and the Imperial City, where the court assembled, amnesties were proclaimed from the Chengtian gate and troops paraded.

roads.name: Chunmingmen Avenue
roads.blurb: The great east-west avenue, 120 m wide, from the Imperial City to the Chunming gate in the east wall, the road to Luoyang. The East Market and Xingqing Palace opened onto it.

roads.name: Jinguangmen Avenue
roads.blurb: The west half of the great cross-avenue, ending at the Jinguang gate, where the Silk Road left the city for Liangzhou, Dunhuang and Samarkand.

roads.name: Avenue before the Imperial City
roads.blurb: The street along the south wall of the Imperial City, joining the three south gates.

roads.name: Yanxingmen-Yanping Avenue
roads.blurb: The southern of the three great cross-avenues, from the Yanxing gate in the east wall to the Yanping gate in the west.

roads.name: Hanguangmen Street
roads.blurb: The avenue south from the Hanguang gate, the west gate of the Imperial City's south wall.

roads.name: Anshangmen Street
roads.blurb: The avenue south from the Anshang gate toward the Qixia gate in the south wall; the Ming South Street later followed its line.

roads.name: Avenue west of the Imperial City
Avenue east of the Imperial City
Danfeng Street
roads.blurb: The broad street (some 120-180 m) running south from the Danfeng gate of the Daming Palace, the court's way down into the city.

roads.name: West Street
roads.blurb: From the Anding gate to the crossing; the Bell Tower of 1384 stood on it near Guangji Street until it was moved east to the crossing in 1582.

roads.name: East Street
roads.blurb: From the crossing to the Changle gate, the road to Lintong and the east.

roads.name: South Street
roads.blurb: On the line of the Tang Anshangmen street, from the crossing to the Yongning (South) gate.

roads.name: Road to Xianyang
roads.blurb: West from the Anding gate across the old wards toward Xianyang and the Gansu corridor: the old Silk Road, now walked by Hui and Central Asian caravans.

roads.name: Road to Ci'en temple
roads.blurb: A country road south from the Yongning gate to the Ci'en temple and its pagoda, past villages on the old wards.

walls.name: Outer wall (guocheng)
walls.blurb: The rammed-earth outer wall of 582, about 36.7 km round and only some 5 m high, with three gates on each of the east, south and west sides. It was a boundary and a customs line more than a fortification.

walls.name: Palace City wall
walls.blurb: The Palace City, 2.8 by 1.5 km: the Taiji Palace in the middle, the Eastern Palace of the crown prince and the Yeting of the palace women on either side, walled in rammed earth about 10 m high.

walls.name: Imperial City wall
walls.blurb: The Imperial City (Huangcheng), 2.8 by 1.8 km, walled on three sides and open to the Hengjie on the north: ministries, courts, the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain, with no private houses. An innovation of the Sui.

walls.name: Daming Palace wall
walls.blurb: The Daming Palace's walls, laid out in 662 as a trapezoid about 7.6 km round on the Longshou plateau, outside the city's north-east wall. The north and its Taiye pond lie beyond the frame.

walls.name: Xingqing Palace wall
walls.blurb: Xuanzong's palace, built from 714 on his princely mansion in the Longqing ward and half the ward north of it.

walls.name: Jiacheng (covered way)
walls.blurb: A walled passage along the east wall, built in the 720s and 730s, by which the emperor could ride unseen from the Daming Palace to the Xingqing Palace and on to the Furong garden at the Qujiang pond.

walls.name: Ming city wall
walls.blurb: Raised in 1370-1378 over the Tang Imperial City's west and south walls and extended north and east: 13.7 km round, 12 m high, with corner towers and barbicans at the four gates. Its rammed earth was faced with brick in 1568; it still stands.

blocks.name: Offices of the Imperial City, west
Offices of the Imperial City, east
Inner halls of the Taiji Palace
Hamlet in the old West Market
Hamlet in the old East Market

gardens.name: West garden of the Taiji Palace
East garden of the Taiji Palace
Fields on the old Daming Palace
Fields east of the Ci'en temple

districts.name: Palace City (Gongcheng)
districts.description: The walled palace at the head of the axis: the Daxing (from Tang times Taiji) Palace of the emperor in the middle, the crown prince's Eastern Palace to the east, the Yeting of the palace women and workshops to the west. The court lived here until the Daming Palace was finished in 663.

districts.name: Imperial City (Huangcheng)
districts.description: The government quarter, a Sui innovation: ministries, courts, the guards' offices, the imperial ancestral temple and the altar of soil and grain, along seven east-west and five north-south streets. No one lived here but officials on duty.

districts.name: Daming Palace
districts.description: The 'Palace of Great Brilliance', the main seat of the Tang court from 663: front halls stepped up the plateau from the Danfeng gate, the inner palace round the Taiye pond to the north.

districts.name: Wannian county (the east)
districts.description: East of Zhuque Avenue the wards belonged to Wannian county (Daxing county under the Sui): higher ground, nearer the Daming Palace, with the mansions of the great, the East Market and the pleasure quarter of Pingkang.

districts.name: Chang'an county (the west)
districts.description: West of the axis, Chang'an county: the West Market and its foreign merchants, Sogdian, Persian and Turkic communities, Zoroastrian and Nestorian temples, and more commoners' wards.

districts.name: Pingkang ward
districts.description: The ward between the Imperial City and the East Market, close to the examination offices: lodgings of candidates and provincial liaison offices, and in its north-east lanes the 'Northern Quarter' of courtesans described by Sun Qi in 884.

districts.name: Xi'an walled city
districts.description: The Ming city of the 1370s: four main streets from four gates, the Prince of Qin's palace in the north-east, garrison quarters, the Hui lanes round the Great Mosque near the Drum Tower.

labels.text: Fields of the old Tang city

periods.label: Daxing, the new Sui capital
periods.summary: Emperor Wen of Sui ordered a new capital in 582 on the plain south-east of the worn-out Han city, and Yuwen Kai laid it out in months: a rammed-earth rectangle 9.7 by 8.6 km, the Palace and Imperial Cities at the head of the axis, two markets, 108 walled wards on a grid of avenues. Halls are timber on earth terraces, tiled in grey.
periods.feel: Fresh-pounded earth walls along avenues far too wide for their traffic, ox-carts of tiles and timber, and wheat growing inside the southern wards.

houses.title: Wards of the new capital
houses.text: Each ward (fang) is a rammed-earth rectangle with two or four gates and a cross of lanes inside. Officials and the families moved in from the old Han city build courtyard compounds of rammed earth and timber near the palace; temples are given whole quarters of wards.

outskirts.title: Empty wards in the south
outskirts.text: South of the markets many wards are walled but hardly lived in: wheat, millet and vegetable plots, a few farmhouses and new temples on the low ridges.

periods.label: Chang'an of Taizong and Gaozong
periods.summary: The Tang took the Sui city whole in 617 and in 618 renamed it Chang'an. Under Taizong and Gaozong it fills: monks back from India, envoys from Japan, Silla and the Western Regions, the Daming Palace raised on the Longshou plateau (begun 634, built 662–663), and in 652 Xuanzang's brick pagoda at the Ci'en temple.
periods.feel: Drums at dawn opening the ward gates, camel bells on the Jinguang avenue, chanting from new temples, and dust from the polo grounds.

houses.title: Courtyard compounds in the wards
houses.text: Behind the ward walls, lanes lead to gated courtyard houses: rammed-earth walls, timber halls under grey tiles, a front court for guests and inner courts for the family. Only officials of the third rank and above may open a gate onto the avenue.

outskirts.title: Gardens of the southern wards
outskirts.text: The southern wards are a patchwork of temple estates, orchards, vegetable gardens and the villas of officials, with fields between their walls.

periods.label: Chang'an, the Tang capital
periods.summary: The capital of a million under Xuanzong: the court at the Daming and Xingqing palaces, Sogdian, Persian and Uighur merchants in the West Market, Nestorian, Manichaean and Zoroastrian temples beside a hundred Buddhist and Taoist ones, Li Bai and Du Fu in the taverns, candidates for the examinations crowding the inns of Pingkang ward.
periods.feel: Pipa music and grape wine from the foreign taverns, the market's noon drum, peonies sold by the cartload in spring, and eight hundred beats of the dusk drums shutting the ward gates.

houses.title: Mansions and lanes of the wards
houses.text: The northern wards hold princes' and ministers' mansions with ponds and pavilions, behind gates on the avenues. Lanes inside the ward walls are lined with shops, inns, wine shops and temples; ordinary houses are one-storey courtyards of earth and timber under grey tiles.

outskirts.title: The thin southern wards
outskirts.text: South of the Yanxing-Yanping avenue, a Song writer recalled, 'though some live there, their kitchen smoke does not join': orchards, fields and temple gardens inside the ward walls.

periods.label: Late Tang Chang'an
periods.summary: The An Lushan rebels took the city in 756 and the Tibetans in 763; the court came back each time, weaker. In 845 Wuzong closed all but four Buddhist temples in the capital and banned the foreign religions. Huang Chao's rebels entered in January 881, and in 904 Zhu Wen pulled the city down and floated its timbers to Luoyang.
periods.feel: Burnt beams among the wards, eunuchs' guards on the avenues, night markets that ignore the curfew, and the scent of peonies the rich still buy at fortunes a stem.

houses.title: Crowded eastern wards
houses.text: Life gathers in the north-east, near the Daming Palace and the East Market: ward walls are breached for shopfronts, houses crowd the lanes, and taverns stay open after the drums. Ruined mansions of the old aristocracy are let out or pulled down.

outskirts.title: Fields in the west and south
outskirts.text: The western and southern wards thin out into fields, ruined temples closed in 845 and vegetable gardens; soldiers camp in deserted compounds.

periods.label: Ming Xi'an
periods.summary: After 904 the city shrank to a walled town on the old Imperial City. The Ming renamed it Xi'an in 1369 and in the 1370s raised new walls on the Tang lines to the west and south, extended north and east, with the palace of the Prince of Qin inside. The Bell Tower (1384) and Drum Tower (1380) mark the centre; the Tang sites are fields and mounds.
periods.feel: Garrison drums from the gate towers, camel trains of the Hui merchants, the reek of tanneries and mutton stalls, and wheat fields running to the foot of the old pagodas.

houses.title: Courtyards of Ming Xi'an
houses.text: Inside the walls, quadrangle houses of grey brick and timber line straight lanes off the four main streets; garrison soldiers live in quarters of their own, the Hui families the lanes round the Great Mosque, merchants the east.

outskirts.title: Villages on the Tang wards
outskirts.text: Outside the walls, villages of loess and brick houses stand among wheat fields on the old wards; the lines of the Tang avenues survive here and there as field roads and village names.

landmarks.name: Taiji Palace: the Taiji Hall

sui-600.name: Daxing Palace: the Daxing Hall
sui-600.note: New: the Sui emperor's palace, named, like the city, after Emperor Wen's old fief of Daxing. The front hall stands on its terrace behind two gates; Wen moved in in 583.

early-tang-650.note: The Tang court's seat until 663. Taizong held court here after the Xuanwu Gate coup of 626 and received envoys from the steppe, who hailed him 'Heavenly Qaghan'.

tang-750.note: Second to the Daming Palace now: used for enthronements, state funerals and some great audiences, its halls kept up by a reduced staff.

late-tang-880.note: Patched after the sacks of 756 and 763 and seldom used. In 904 Zhu Wen will have its timbers pulled down and floated to Luoyang.

ming-1400.note: Gone. The Ming north wall cuts across the site; the Tang terraces lie under fields and the houses of the north of the city.

landmarks.summary: The main hall of the Sui-Tang Palace City on the city's axis: a great hipped hall on a rammed-earth terrace, behind the Taiji gate and its cloistered court.
details: Built 582-583 as the Daxing Palace by Yuwen Kai, it was the throne hall of the first Tang emperors: Gaozu, Taizong and the young Gaozong held the dawn audiences here on the first and fifteenth of the month. Behind it lay the Liangyi Hall and the inner palace, with ponds and gardens to the north.

Almost nothing has been excavated under modern Xi'an, so the miniature is an interpretation: a hall of eleven bays with a hipped roof and ridge-end ornaments, the Taiji gate and the cloister, after the Daming Palace's excavated halls and Tang tomb paintings of palace architecture.
landmarks.function: Throne hall of the Palace City

landmarks.name: Chengtian Gate

sui-600.name: Guangyang Gate
sui-600.note: New: the south gate of the Daxing Palace, probably called Guangyang under the Sui, with three passages through its earth platform.

early-tang-650.note: Here the emperor proclaimed amnesties, received captive kings and watched the New Year festivities on the Hengjie square below.

tang-750.note: Still the stage for amnesties and triumphs; the court now spends most of its time in the Daming and Xingqing palaces.

late-tang-880.note: Damaged in the fighting of the 880s and pulled down with the palace in 904.

ming-1400.note: Gone. Its site, excavated in part, lies inside the Ming city's northern quarter.

landmarks.summary: The front gate of the Palace City, a three-passage gate under a long timber hall with flanking towers, facing the 220 m Hengjie square.
details: The gate was the ceremonial threshold of the state: from its tower the emperor proclaimed amnesties, held the 'great audience' at New Year and the winter solstice, and watched victory parades. A golden cock on a pole was raised before it when an amnesty was read.

The miniature shows a reconstruction from excavations of the gate's base, of other Tang palace gates and of tomb murals: three passages in a brick-faced earth platform, a seven-bay hall above and side towers linked by covered ways. The tower details are conjecture.
landmarks.function: Main south gate of the Palace City

landmarks.name: Zhuque Gate

sui-600.note: New: the central south gate of the Imperial City, facing 5 km down Zhuque Avenue to the Mingde gate.

early-tang-650.note: In 645 the crowds that met Xuanzang's sutras packed the avenue in front of it; in 648 a great procession carried them to the new Ci'en temple.

tang-750.note: Its gatekeepers opened at the dawn drums; examination candidates passed through to the Ministry of Rites inside.

late-tang-880.note: Behind it the ministries keep working, with fewer clerks and less revenue, through rebellion and recovery.

ming-1400.note: Gone. The Ming south wall follows the Tang wall line; excavation has found the gate's foundations.

landmarks.summary: The middle gate of the Imperial City's south wall, the head of Zhuque Avenue: three passages through a rammed-earth gate platform under a timber gate tower.
details: The gate joined the government quarter to the 150 m avenue, the city's ceremonial axis. Envoys entered here on their way to the palace, and the court sometimes held banquets for the people on the avenue in front of it.

Excavation found the base of a three-passage gate; the upper structure here follows the standard reconstruction of Tang city gates, with a five-bay hall under a hipped roof on the wall. The flanking wall stubs are shortened.
landmarks.function: South gate of the Imperial City

landmarks.name: Danfeng Gate of the Daming Palace

sui-600.note: Not yet. The city's north wall runs here, with the Forbidden Park beyond it on the Longshou plateau.

early-tang-650.note: New in 662-663 with Gaozong's rebuilding of the palace: the five-passage front gate in the city's north wall, opening onto the broad Danfeng Street.

tang-750.note: The court's front door. Amnesties were proclaimed from its tower, and new emperors showed themselves here after their accession.

late-tang-880.note: The palace was burned and plundered in the wars of the 880s and 890s, and the gate went with it.

ming-1400.note: Gone, its base buried under the loess south of the palace mound. Excavated in 2005 and roofed over by a protective hall in 2010.

landmarks.summary: The main south gate of the Daming Palace, with five passages, the most of any Tang gate, set in the city's north wall at the head of Danfeng Street.
details: Excavation in 2005 found a gate base about 75 m long and 33 m deep with five passages, each some 8.5 m wide, flanked by ramps up to the wall walk. Only the Mingde gate, the city's main south gate, shared the five openings; most gates had three or one.

The miniature shows the excavated plan with an upper hall of eleven bays, flanking stretches of wall and ramp. The form of the gate tower is reconstructed from murals and Tang building rules and is not known in detail.
landmarks.function: Front gate of the Daming Palace

landmarks.name: Hanyuan Hall of the Daming Palace

sui-600.note: Not yet. The Longshou plateau lies outside the walls in the Forbidden Park.

early-tang-650.note: Taizong began a summer palace here for his father in 634, abandoned when Gaozu died in 635. Gaozong built the Daming Palace in 662-663 and this great front hall was finished in 663.

tang-750.note: The stage of New Year and winter-solstice audiences: envoys from Japan, Silla, the Turks and the Arabs climbed the Dragon-Tail Way to the emperor's throne.

late-tang-880.note: Still standing. In January 881 Huang Chao is said to have proclaimed himself emperor of Qi in this hall; it was destroyed in the wars of the following years.

ming-1400.name: Mound of the Hanyuan Hall
ming-1400.note: A worn terrace of rammed earth among wheat fields north of the city; villagers dig it for building earth.

landmarks.summary: The front throne hall of the Daming Palace, raised on a three-tiered rammed-earth terrace at the tip of the Longshou plateau, flanked by two towers and approached by the long ramps of the Dragon-Tail Way.
details: Excavation in 1995-96 found the terrace, the hall of eleven by four bays (about 67 by 29 m inside its gallery), the Xiangluan and Qifeng towers on spurs to either side and the three parallel ramps, some 70 m long, rising in stages to the hall.

The miniature follows Fu Xinian's reconstruction: a hipped roof of grey tile with ridge-end fins, red columns, white walls, triple-tiered towers linked by flying corridors, all on brick-faced earth platforms. The heights are estimates; the ramps are simplified to three straight flights.
landmarks.function: Front hall of state of the Daming Palace: New Year audiences, receptions of envoys

landmarks.name: East Market (Dongshi)

sui-600.name: Dushui Market
sui-600.note: New: the Sui eastern market, called Dushui, laid out over two wards with its own walls, four gates and a grid of lanes.

early-tang-650.note: Renamed East Market. Its 220 trades (hang), each in its own row, sell to the officials and aristocrats of the eastern wards.

tang-750.note: Shops of the great families, printers of calendars and almanacs, iron-mongers, butchers and wine shops; the noon drum opens it and three hundred gong strokes close it before sunset.

late-tang-880.note: A fire in 843 burned some 4,000 houses and shops of the market; it was rebuilt, and night trading now goes on in the wards around it.

ming-1400.note: Gone. A few hamlets and fields cover the site east of the Ming walls.

landmarks.summary: One of the two great walled markets of Chang'an, two wards in size: lanes of shops in rows by trade round a market office, under strict hours and price controls.
details: The market measured about 920 by 1,000 m inside walls, with gates on all four sides and two lanes each way, about 30 m wide, dividing it into nine blocks. Shops faced the lanes and the inside of the walls. The market office checked weights and prices, and a pond and a well served the stalls.

The miniature follows the excavated plan in outline; the rows of shops and the market office are generic, with stall roofs and awnings simplified. The density of building inside the blocks is guessed.
landmarks.function: Official market of the eastern city

landmarks.name: West Market (Xishi)

sui-600.name: Liren Market
sui-600.note: New: the Sui western market, called Liren, the twin of the eastern market across the axis.

early-tang-650.note: The end of the Silk Road: Sogdian, Turkic and Persian caravans unload here, and the market fills with horses, jade, glass and spices.

tang-750.note: The 'Golden Market' of the poets: Sogdian wine shops with western serving girls, Persian jewellers, money shops holding deposits, and timber brought by a new canal of 742 to a pond in the market.

late-tang-880.note: Poorer since the Tibetans took the Gansu corridor and the Western Regions between the 760s and 790s, and many foreigners left after 845; still the city's busiest market.

ming-1400.note: Gone, a hamlet and fields west of the Ming walls. Its site was excavated before the Tang West Market Museum was built over part of it.

landmarks.summary: The western market, larger in trade than the eastern: the end of the Silk Road, where Sogdian, Persian and Uighur merchants sold horses, silver, gems and wine.
details: The plan matched the East Market: walls about 930 by 1,030 m, four gates, a grid of lanes and blocks of shops facing them, with the market office and the office for weights at the centre. Excavations found the lanes, drains, shops and a bridge over a ditch; Tang texts mention a pond for releasing living creatures.

As with the East Market the miniature is schematic: the walls, gates and lanes after excavation, the rows of shops generic. The timber pond in the south-east corner follows texts about the canal of 742; its exact place is uncertain.
landmarks.function: Official market of the western city

landmarks.name: Xingqing Palace and the Dragon Pond

early-tang-650.note: Not yet. The Longqing ward is houses and lanes; a well here is said to have overflowed in the 690s and spread into a pond, the later Dragon Pond.

tang-750.note: Xuanzong's favourite residence since 728: here Yang Guifei viewed peonies at the Chenxiang Pavilion and Li Bai wrote his three Qingping songs for her, and the emperor's birthday was feasted from the tower over the avenue.

late-tang-880.note: The retired Xuanzong was moved out of it in 760; later the home of dowager empresses, little used and sacked with the rest of the city in the 880s.

ming-1400.note: Gone, fields east of the city wall. The pond was dug out again in the 1950s for a public park on the site.

landmarks.summary: The palace Xuanzong made from his princely mansion: halls in the north, the Dragon Pond in the south with the Chenxiang Pavilion of agarwood, and towers overlooking the Chunming avenue.
details: Li Longji and his brothers lived in the Longqing ward as princes; after his accession in 712 the ward became a palace (from 714), enlarged with half the ward to the north and joined to the Daming Palace by the covered way along the city wall. The Huae Xianghui and Qinzheng Wubenlou towers in its south-west corner looked onto the avenue.

The miniature shows a portion: the pond, the Chenxiang Pavilion on its terrace, the two towers by the wall and the main halls behind. The layout follows a Song stone map of the palace and partial excavation; the buildings are reconstructions.
landmarks.function: Palace and pleasure ground of Xuanzong

landmarks.name: Greater Wild Goose Pagoda (Da Ci'en Temple)

sui-600.note: Not yet. The Sui Wulou temple stands in the Jinchang ward; in 648 the crown prince Li Zhi will refound it as Da Ci'en, 'Great Maternal Grace', for his dead mother.

early-tang-650.note: New in 652: Xuanzang's own pagoda for the sutras and relics he brought from India, five storeys of brick over an earth core on a high square base, in the west court of the temple.

tang-750.note: Rebuilt in 701-704, probably to seven storeys (some sources say ten); new jinshi graduates climb it and write their names on its walls, a custom said to begin in the 700s.

late-tang-880.note: One of only four temples left open in the capital after 845, with thirty monks; the peonies of its courts are famous.

ming-1400.note: The pagoda stands in fields south of the city, the temple shrunk to a few halls. It will be cased in a new skin of brick in 1604.

landmarks.summary: The square brick pagoda Xuanzang raised in 652 to keep the sutras he brought from India, rebuilt in 701-704 as the seven storeys that still stand 64 m high.
details: Xuanzang returned in 645 with 657 texts and worked in the temple's translation court. His first pagoda, imitating Indian models with an earth core faced in brick, decayed within decades; Empress Wu's court rebuilt it in brick in 701-704. Its plain walls are divided by shallow pilasters, with an arched opening in each face of every storey.

The 750 model shows the pagoda on its platform with the west court's cloister and halls. The 652 pagoda is reconstructed from texts only (five storeys, about 54 m). The Ming casing of 1604 and the present halls are later; the temple's Tang plan is largely unknown.
landmarks.function: Pagoda of the Da Ci'en temple, repository of Xuanzang's sutras

landmarks.name: Lesser Wild Goose Pagoda (Jianfu Temple)

early-tang-650.note: Not yet. The Jianfu temple will be founded in 684 in the Kaihua ward across the street for the soul of Emperor Gaozong.

tang-750.note: Built in 707-709 in the temple's southern court in the Anren ward: fifteen storeys of brick, about 45 m, beside the hall where the monk Yijing translated the scriptures he brought back by sea.

late-tang-880.note: Jianfu was one of the four temples spared in 845; the pagoda rises over a half-empty city.

ming-1400.note: Still complete with its fifteen storeys. A local legend says the earthquake of 1487 split it from top to bottom and another closed the crack in 1521; the top two storeys fell in 1555.

landmarks.summary: A slender dense-eaved brick pagoda of fifteen storeys, built in 707-709 for the Jianfu temple, its eaves corbelled out in courses of brick and its outline swelling gently before narrowing to the top.
details: The pagoda stands on a square base about 11 m a side; a tall first storey with arched doors on the north and south carries fourteen low storeys, each a band of wall under a cornice of stepped brick courses. Its profile curves like a spindle, the classic shape of Tang dense-eave pagodas.

The miniature shows it complete as in Tang and Ming times, with fifteen storeys and a simple finial, in a walled court with the Jianfu temple bell tower and a hall. The court is reconstructed; only the pagoda and later Ming-Qing halls survive.
landmarks.function: Pagoda of the Jianfu temple

landmarks.name: Daxingshan Temple

sui-600.note: New: the Sui state temple, given the whole Jingshan ward on the fifth of the six ridges, facing the Taoist Xuandu abbey across Zhuque Avenue.

early-tang-650.note: A centre of translation since the Sui, when the Indian monk Narendrayasas worked here with Chinese scribes.

tang-750.note: Soon the temple of the Tantric master Amoghavajra (d. 774), with esoteric rites for the protection of the state.

late-tang-880.note: Closed in 845 and its monks laicised; probably reopened after 846, smaller and poorer.

ming-1400.note: A small temple on the old site among fields; the present halls are mostly Ming and Qing rebuilding.

landmarks.summary: The great state temple of the Sui, filling a whole ward on Zhuque Avenue: a gate, a pagoda and a main hall on the axis, cloistered courts of monks' quarters around them.
details: Emperor Wen built it with the city, as the head temple of his Buddhist state, and gave it the city's own name, Daxing. Its counterpart, the Taoist Xuandu abbey, was set opposite so that no commoner's house would stand on the ridge that geomancers likened to the fifth line of the trigram qian.

Little of the Tang temple is known in plan. The miniature is an interpretation of a large Tang monastery: gate, middle gate, a timber pagoda, the Buddha hall in a cloistered court and the lecture hall behind, with monks' quarters round the edges.
landmarks.function: State Buddhist temple

landmarks.name: Xuandu Abbey

sui-600.note: New in 582: the Taoist state abbey, moved here from the old Han city and placed opposite the Daxingshan temple on the fifth ridge.

early-tang-650.note: The Tang emperors claimed descent from Laozi, Li Er; Taoist abbeys like this rank before Buddhist temples at court.

tang-750.note: Xuanzong's age: the emperor annotates the Daodejing, and the abbey's priests perform rites of the Golden Register for the state.

late-tang-880.note: Taoists are in favour under Wuzong, whose Taoist advisers urged the persecution of 845; the abbeys are spared while the temples fall.

ming-1400.note: Gone; its site in the fields south-west of the city.

landmarks.summary: The Sui-Tang state Taoist abbey on Zhuque Avenue, the counterpart of the Daxingshan temple: a halls-and-courts complex with an altar platform and towers for the scriptures.
details: The abbey occupied a large part of the Chongye ward and kept the Taoist canon. Its priests performed the state's offerings to the Heavenly Worthies and to Laozi, the dynasty's claimed ancestor. Its plan is not known; Tang Taoist abbeys followed Buddhist temple plans with halls on an axis, galleries and a gate.
The miniature is an interpretation: a gate, a three-tiered altar for the great rites, the main hall of the Three Pure Ones and two scripture towers, in a walled court.
landmarks.function: State Taoist abbey

landmarks.name: Ximing Temple

sui-600.note: Not yet. The north-east corner of the Yankang ward is the mansion of the Sui minister Yang Su.

early-tang-650.note: New in 656-658: Gaozong built the temple on the old mansion for the recovery of his crown prince, with Xuanzang among its first monks; its plan was said to copy the Jetavana of India.

tang-750.note: One of the city's great teaching temples; the Japanese monk Dōji is said to have studied here and to have modelled Nara's Daian-ji on its plan.

late-tang-880.note: One of the four temples kept open in the capital in 845, with thirty monks.

ming-1400.note: Gone, under fields; part of its plan was excavated in 1985.

landmarks.summary: A great Tang temple in the Yankang ward founded by Gaozong in 656-658: a series of cloistered courts with a main hall, lecture hall and pagoda, and a famous library.
details: Ximing was one of the largest temples of Chang'an, with some ten courts and thousands of bays of buildings. Xuanzang lived here in 658, and the vinaya master Daoxuan wrote here. Excavation in 1985 found part of the eastern courts with halls and corridors.
The miniature shows the central axis as a reconstruction: a gate, the main hall in a cloister, a lecture hall and a pagoda, with side courts suggested.
landmarks.function: State Buddhist temple

landmarks.name: Da Qin Monastery (Church of the East)

sui-600.note: Not yet. The Yining ward is houses and gardens near the Jinguang gate.

early-tang-650.name: Persian Monastery (Bosi si)
early-tang-650.note: New: the monk Aluoben came from Persia in 635 with Syriac scriptures; Taizong had a monastery built for him in the Yining ward in 638, with 21 monks.

tang-750.note: Renamed Da Qin ('Roman') monastery in 745 to distinguish the Christians from the Persian Zoroastrians. Its monks serve Persian and Sogdian Christians and some Chinese converts.

late-tang-880.note: The stele of 781 still stands in the court, but the monastery was closed in 845 with all foreign temples; the buildings stand empty or are let out.

ming-1400.note: Gone. The stele, perhaps buried at the persecution, will be dug up near Xi'an around 1625 and caused a sensation among the Jesuits.

landmarks.summary: The first Christian church in China, of the Church of the East, in the Yining ward near the west gate: a small temple-style compound where in 781 the great stele recording its history was set up.
details: The stele of 781, carved in Chinese and Syriac, tells how Aluoben brought the 'luminous teaching' in 635 and how emperors favoured it, and lists some seventy clergy. Tang Christians used Buddhist and Taoist words for their faith; the monastery looked like a Chinese temple, with a cross set on its roof perhaps.

The miniature is an interpretation: a gate, a main hall and a court with the stele on a tortoise base, as Tang steles commonly stood. The site of the monastery in the ward is approximate, and its buildings are not known.
landmarks.function: Monastery of the Church of the East

landmarks.name: Imperial Academy (Guozijian)

sui-600.note: New: the Sui directorate of education in the Wuben ward, just south of the Imperial City's Anshang gate.

early-tang-650.note: Under Taizong the Academy grew to over 3,000 students, among them sons of the nobles of Koguryo, Paekche, Silla, Gaochang and Tibet.

tang-750.note: Its six schools teach the classics, law, calligraphy and mathematics; Abe no Nakamaro studied here before entering the Tang service.

late-tang-880.note: In 837 the Kaicheng stone classics, twelve classics cut on 114 stones, were set up here; they survive in Xi'an's Forest of Steles.

ming-1400.note: Gone; the Kaicheng classics were moved inside the city walls and are kept today in the Forest of Steles (Beilin).

landmarks.summary: The Imperial Academy, the state's college for the classics, beside the Temple of Confucius in the Wuben ward: lecture halls, dormitories and libraries in walled courts.
details: The directorate ran the Schools for the Sons of the State, the Great School, the School of the Four Gates and the schools of law, calligraphy and mathematics. Students lived in dormitories, sat monthly tests and could be expelled for failure or misconduct; the best went on to the examinations.
The miniature is an interpretation: a gate, the Confucian temple hall and its court, a lecture hall, two rows of dormitories and a library. The layout of the Tang Academy is not known.
landmarks.function: Imperial Academy and Temple of Confucius

landmarks.name: Yongning Gate and the Ming walls

late-tang-880.note: Not yet. Here stood the Tang Imperial City's Anshang gate; after 904 the shrunken city kept the Imperial City's walls.

ming-1400.note: New in the 1370s: the south gate of Ming Xi'an, with a gate tower, an arrow tower on the barbican and a bridge over the moat.

landmarks.summary: The south gate of the Ming walls, on the line of the Tang Imperial City: a gate tower on the wall, a square barbican and an arrow tower facing the moat.
details: Zhu Yuanzhang's son Zhu Shuang, Prince of Qin, held Xi'an from 1378. The walls were raised in 1370-1378 on the Tang walls to the west and south and extended north and east, 12 m high, 15-18 m thick at the base and 12-14 m at the top. The gate towers and barbicans are of the Ming; the brick facing of the whole wall dates from 1568.

The miniature shows the gate as rebuilt later in the Ming and as it stands today, with the earth wall faced in brick; in 1400 the wall's face was probably still bare rammed earth. The drawbridge tower in front is omitted.
landmarks.function: South gate of the Ming city

landmarks.name: Bell Tower

late-tang-880.note: Not yet. The ruined Imperial City's offices stand here.

ming-1400.note: New in 1384: built near Guangji Street at the centre of the older city, it rang the hours for the city; it was moved a few hundred metres east to the crossing of the four main streets in 1582.

landmarks.summary: The Ming bell tower of 1384, a three-eaved timber pavilion with a pointed roof on a square brick base pierced by four arched passages.
details: The tower stood first at the Yingxiang temple on West Street; in 1582 it was taken down and rebuilt at the new centre of the enlarged city, where it still stands. Its base is about 35 m square and 8.6 m high; the timber tower above, with three tiers of eaves under green-glazed tiles and a gilded finial, rises to some 36 m.
The miniature shows the present building, assumed close to the 1384 form. Its bell, rung at dawn, answered the drum of the Drum Tower at dusk.
landmarks.function: Bell tower marking the hours

landmarks.name: Drum Tower

late-tang-880.note: Not yet.

ming-1400.note: New in 1380: the drum that beat the dusk and the night watches over the Ming city, on a brick platform with an arched passage.

landmarks.summary: The Ming drum tower of 1380: a long two-storey timber hall with three tiers of eaves and a hip-and-gable roof on a brick platform with an arched road through it.
details: The platform is about 53 by 38 m and 7.7 m high; the timber tower, with a balcony round its upper storey, rises to about 34 m. A great drum on the upper floor beat the dusk and the watches; it stands on the street to the Great Mosque, in the Hui quarter.
The miniature shows the present building, restored many times, without the rows of drums placed round the gallery today.
landmarks.function: Drum tower beating the dusk and the night watches

landmarks.name: Great Mosque of Xi'an

late-tang-880.note: Tradition dates a mosque here to 742, under Xuanzong; there is no contemporary evidence, though Muslim merchants were living in Chang'an by then.

ming-1400.note: Rebuilt or enlarged under the Hongwu emperor, perhaps in 1392 (the date is traditional): a mosque in the form of a Chinese temple of courts, gates and pavilions.

landmarks.summary: A mosque built as a Chinese temple: four courts on an east-west axis, wooden archways, a pagoda-like octagonal minaret pavilion, and the prayer hall at the west end facing Mecca.
details: The mosque is about 250 m long and 50 m wide. Visitors pass through a wooden archway, a stone archway, a court with a three-storey octagonal pavilion (the Shengxin tower, used to call to prayer), and a phoenix pavilion before the prayer hall, roofed in blue-green glazed tiles, whose inside is carved with Arabic calligraphy.
Most present buildings are Ming and Qing. The miniature shows the full four-court plan as it stood in the later Ming; in 1400 parts of it may not yet have been built.
landmarks.function: Friday mosque of the Hui community

landmarks.name: Palace of the Prince of Qin

late-tang-880.note: Not yet. Here were the wards east of the Palace City.

ming-1400.note: New in the 1370s: the walled palace of Zhu Shuang, Prince of Qin, second son of the Hongwu emperor, a city within the city with its own moat and gates.

landmarks.summary: The Ming palace of the Princes of Qin in the north-east of Xi'an: a moated, walled inner palace with three main halls on an axis, inside an outer walled precinct.
details: Zhu Shuang was enfeoffed as Prince of Qin in 1370 and came to Xi'an in 1378; the palace, among the first and grandest of the Ming princely palaces, was built in the 1370s. The princes of Qin held it until the city fell to Li Zicheng in 1643. Fragments of its earth walls survive round the modern Xincheng square.

The miniature is a reconstruction after the rules for princely palaces in the Ming statutes and the later palace plans: double walls with a moat between, a gate, three halls on a terrace and the residential halls behind.
landmarks.function: Palace of the Prince of Qin

spots.name: A Sogdian wine shop east of the West Market
spots.summary: One of the 'foreign-girl' wine shops (huji jiusi) by the West Market, where Sogdian women poured grape wine and western dancers whirled to drums and pipa.
details: Poets placed these taverns 'east of the Golden Market': Li Bai's young gallants, their silver saddles in the spring wind, 'laugh their way into the foreign girls' wine shops'. Grape wine came from Gaochang and was made in the capital too. The whirling Sogdian dance (huxuan), performed on a small round rug, was a craze at court and in the taverns.

vignettes.text: Shutters come down at the noon drum. A Sogdian woman with green eyes and a red silk skirt sets out amber cups and jars of grape wine on the counter.
Young men of good family tie their horses at the gate. A dancer spins on a round rug, faster and faster, to a drum and a curved pipa, sleeves flying.
The dusk drums start. The drinkers must be home inside their own ward walls before the last beat, or spend the night here with the wine.

late-tang-880.note: Fewer Sogdians since the An Lushan rebellion, led by a general of Sogdian descent, turned the city against westerners; Uighur traders now run many wine shops and moneylenders.

spots.name: A camel caravan on the Jinguang avenue
spots.summary: A caravan of Bactrian camels arriving from the Jinguang gate with silver, glass, spices and horses from the Western Regions, bound for the caravanserais beside the West Market.
details: Caravans came up the Gansu corridor from Dunhuang and Liangzhou, with passes checked at every barrier. Sogdian caravan leaders (sabao) carried silver, glass, perfumes, saffron and horses west to east, and silk the other way. Tang tomb figurines show the camels loaded with rolls of silk, flasks and even musicians riding on their backs.

vignettes.text: The dawn drums open the Jinguang gate. Forty camels kneel in the dust while clerks check the travel passes, one by one, against a list of names and loads.
Bales of felt, bags of pepper, a crate of Persian glass and two Ferghana horses are led down the avenue toward the West Market.
In the caravanserai yard the camels are unloaded and watered. A Sogdian merchant counts silver coins of the Persian king and burns incense at a little fire altar.

tang-750.note: At its height: Sogdian, Persian and Turkic caravans, and Tang troops holding the oasis cities as far as Kucha and Kashgar.

spots.name: Money shops by the West Market
spots.summary: Deposit shops (guifang) by the West Market, where merchants left silver and strings of copper coins against written receipts, and lenders, many of them foreign, charged steep interest.
details: Copper cash was heavy: a string of a thousand coins weighed some 4 kg. Deposit shops stored money and paid on a written order, and by the 800s merchants used 'flying money' (feiqian), drafts drawn on provincial offices in the capital. Uighur moneylenders were notorious, and the court repeatedly banned loans from foreigners to officials.

vignettes.text: A cart of copper strings is unloaded under guard. The clerk weighs a silver ingot, writes a receipt with the shop's seal and stores the silver in a chest bound with iron.
A young official, deep in debt from his examination banquets, borrows against his next salary at a monthly rate he does not like to say out loud.
The gong will soon close the market. The shopkeeper counts the day's coins on an abacus and locks the strong room under the floor.

late-tang-880.note: Merchants now send money by 'flying money' drafts; a fire of 843 in the East Market showed how much wealth sat in the shops.

spots.name: Li Bai's wine shop
spots.summary: A wine shop in the market wards where Li Bai, court poet from 742 to 744, drank and slept: Du Fu wrote that he 'made a hundred poems for a dipper of wine, and slept in a tavern in the market of Chang'an'.
details: Li Bai came to court in 742 and served in the Hanlin academy; the stories say the emperor once had him sobered with cold water to write songs for Yang Guifei. He left in 744. Du Fu's 'Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup' pictures him refusing the emperor's summons from a tavern. Where he drank is not known; the marker is placed in the wards east of the West Market.

vignettes.text: A wine-seller stirs a vat of cloudy rice wine. A tall man in a court robe already has three empty jars on his table and calls for brush and paper.
A eunuch from the palace arrives with a summons; the poet waves him away. 'Your servant is an immortal of the wine,' he says, and turns back to his cup.
The drums have long finished. The poet sleeps where he fell, his poem pasted on the wall, and the shopkeeper shutters the doors around him.

spots.name: A candidate's lodging in Pingkang ward
spots.summary: A room let to a provincial candidate for the jinshi examination in Pingkang ward, between the Ministry of Rites and the East Market, where the courtesans of the 'Northern Quarter' also lived.
details: Candidates came to the capital each autumn, lodged near the examination halls, called on officials with scrolls of their poems ('warming the scroll') and sat the examinations in early spring. Perhaps thirty of a thousand passed. Sun Qi's Record of the Northern Quarter (884) describes the courtesans' houses in the ward's north-east lanes, their drinking games and the new graduates' parties.

vignettes.text: The candidate copies his best poems onto a fresh scroll by lamplight, to leave at the gate of a minister who might put in a good word with the examiner.
Results are out. A friend who passed is carried off to a feast in the Northern Quarter; the candidate who failed sits in his room composing a poem of complaint.
Behind the ward walls the courtesans' houses are lit. The drums have shut the ward gates, but inside Pingkang the music and drinking games go on.

late-tang-880.note: The Northern Quarter at its most famous; Sun Qi will write it up in 884 from memories of these years, after Huang Chao's sack.

spots.name: Street drums at the Chongren ward gate
spots.summary: The drums on the avenues that opened and closed the ward and market gates: at dusk 800 beats, and anyone still in the streets after them broke the curfew.
details: Under Taizong the patrolling criers were replaced by street drums at the posts on the main avenues, answering a drum beaten at the palace (in the 630s, on Ma Zhou's proposal). At dusk the drums beat 800 times and the ward gates closed; at the fifth watch they beat again and the gates opened. The Tang code set twenty strokes of the light stick for being out after curfew.

vignettes.text: The fifth watch. A drum sounds from the palace, then from the post on the avenue, and the gatekeeper of Chongren ward lifts the bar of the gate.
The first dusk beats roll down the Chunming avenue. Carts hurry, hawkers fold up, an official whips his horse to reach his own ward in time.
Silence on the avenues. A patrol of the city guard stops a man without a pass, a doctor called to a birth, and lets him go with a warning.

late-tang-880.note: The rules slip: night markets open inside the wards, and shops break through the ward walls onto the streets.

spots.name: A silk merchant of the East Market
spots.summary: A silk shop in the East Market's row of silk dealers, selling plain tabby, damask and gauze to the households of the eastern wards and to merchants bound for the west.
details: Bolts of plain silk were also money: taxes, salaries and big purchases were paid in silk as well as copper. A standard bolt was about 12 m long. Dealers of a trade had their shops together in one row (hang) under a head of the row responsible to the market office, which checked prices three times a month.

vignettes.text: The noon drum. The silk dealer unrolls a bolt of figured damask for the steward of a prince's household, who rubs it between finger and thumb.
A Sogdian buyer pays for forty bolts of plain silk with silver and a horse. The head of the silk row witnesses the contract.
The gong strokes. The shop is shuttered and the apprentice counts the remaining bolts against the ledger before the market gates close.

spots.name: Sesame-cake (hubing) oven in Fuxing ward
spots.summary: An oven baking hubing, the flat sesame-crusted 'foreign cakes' that Chang'an ate for breakfast; Bai Juyi, sending some from the provinces, asked whether they tasted like those of Fuxing ward.
details: Wheat flatbreads baked in clay ovens came from Central Asia and became the city's daily bread. In 756, fleeing the rebels, Xuanzong is said to have eaten hubing bought by Yang Guozhong in a market. Bai Juyi's poem of the 810s praises cakes 'crisp outside, fragrant with oil, fresh from the oven' in the capital style. The ward's position is approximate.

vignettes.text: Before the gates open the baker slaps rounds of dough sprinkled with sesame onto the hot inner wall of a clay oven, then hooks them out puffed and brown.
Officials on their way to the dawn audience buy a hot cake through the shop window and eat it in the saddle.
The day's last batch goes to a monastery kitchen and to the soldiers of the gate guard.

spots.name: Abe no Nakamaro's lodging
spots.summary: The Japanese student Abe no Nakamaro, who came with the embassy of 717, studied at the Academy, entered the Tang service as Chao Heng and became a friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei.
details: Nakamaro served in the palace library and the guards and rose to high office. In 753 he set out for home with the embassy of Fujiwara no Kiyokawa; his ship was wrecked on the coast of Annam, Li Bai wrote a lament thinking him drowned, and he returned to Chang'an, dying there in 770. The marker stands for the Court of State Ceremonial in the Imperial City, which handled foreign envoys.

vignettes.text: Chao Heng, in the green robe of a Tang official, rides to his office in the palace library past the guards at the Anfu gate.
An embassy from Japan has arrived. He interprets for the envoys at the Court of State Ceremonial and hears news of home after thirty years.
In his lodging he looks up at the moon and thinks of Mount Mikasa at Kasuga, which he left as a youth.

spots.name: Peony sellers in spring
spots.summary: The peony craze of late Tang Chang'an: for three weeks each spring the city bought tree peonies by the cart, and a single clump of dark flowers could cost the taxes of ten households.
details: Bai Juyi's poem 'Buying Flowers' describes the crowds going 'like mad' after peonies at the end of spring, carts and horses jostling, and an old farmer sighing that one clump of deep-red blooms costs as much as the taxes of ten middle households. The Ci'en temple's peonies and those of the great mansions drew sightseers across the city.

vignettes.text: Gardeners from the southern wards bring peonies in tubs on hand-carts, wrapped against the dust, the buds just opening.
A steward haggles for a purple 'many-petalled' plant for his master's garden. The price would buy a family's grain for a year.
The flower sellers shade their plants with mats. Young men ride by with a single blossom in their caps.

spots.name: Xuanzang's translation court at the Ci'en temple
spots.summary: The translation bureau where Xuanzang and a team of learned monks turned the Sanskrit texts he brought from India into Chinese, from 648 at the new Ci'en temple.
details: The work was organised like a government office: Xuanzang read and rendered the Sanskrit aloud, while monks checked meaning and grammar, scribes wrote, stylists polished the Chinese and others verified it against the original. In nineteen years he translated 75 works in 1,335 scrolls. He moved from the Hongfu temple to the Ci'en temple in 648; the court's exact place in the temple is not known.

vignettes.text: The master has already set the day's quota of verses. He reads a line of Sanskrit from a palm-leaf book and gives its sense in Chinese; a scribe writes it down.
A monk who knows grammar disputes a word; the master explains. A stylist reads the polished sentence aloud for the ear.
By lamplight the master marks tomorrow's passage and recites his evening devotions; he rises before dawn to work again, the biography says.

spots.name: Polo ground of the Daming Palace
spots.summary: A polo ground in the western part of the Daming Palace, where emperors, princes and guards played the game the Tang learned from Persia via Central Asia.
details: Polo came to China from Persia through the Turks and Tibetans. Xuanzong as a prince led a team that beat a Tibetan side in 710, and several Tang emperors played obsessively; one, Jingzong, was killed after a night of polo in 826. A stone inscription of 831 found near the palace records the building of a hall and polo ground.

vignettes.text: Grooms roll and water the beaten-earth field. Ponies from Ferghana stamp in their stalls; a groom paints the wooden balls red.
The emperor's team in purple against the guards in green: sticks clash, the ball flies, the crowd of eunuchs and court ladies cheers from the pavilion.
Lamps are lit round the field. A prince insists on another chukka in the dark; the horses steam in the cooling air.

late-tang-880.note: Late Tang emperors play harder than ever; Xizong, the emperor of 880, is said to have boasted that he would come first in a polo examination.

spots.name: Rammed-earth crews on the ward walls
spots.summary: Conscript labourers building the walls of a new ward: earth pounded layer by layer between wooden boards, the method used for every wall in Daxing from the city wall down.
details: The city was laid out and walled with astonishing speed: begun in the sixth month of 582, it received the court in the third month of 583. Walls were built of loess rammed in layers 8-10 cm thick between shuttering boards; the ward walls were some 2.5-3 m thick at the base. Many wards in the south stayed half-empty for decades.

vignettes.text: A foreman snaps a line along the trench. Men fill the space between two rows of boards with loess and tramp it down with stone-headed rammers, singing to keep time.
Another layer done. The boards are lifted and set higher; the wall's side shows thin stripes of each layer, like a cut cake.
The crew from another county takes its rations of millet in the half-built ward. Beyond the wall a farmer still ploughs his old field.

spots.name: The night watch at the crossing
spots.summary: The watchmen of Ming Xi'an at the crossing of the four main streets, answering the Bell Tower's dawn bell and the Drum Tower's dusk drum and calling the night watches.
details: Ming cities kept a curfew enforced by watchmen and the garrison. The bell rang at dawn and the drum at dusk, the 'morning bell and evening drum' of Chinese cities; the watches were struck on drums or wooden clappers through the night. Xi'an was also a frontier garrison city, with the troops of several guard units quartered inside the walls.

vignettes.text: The bell sounds from the tower near Guangji Street. Gatekeepers at the four gates draw the bolts; carts of vegetables wait on the moat bridges.
The Drum Tower's drum beats the dusk. Shopkeepers on East Street put up their shutters; a watchman lights the lantern at his post.
The second watch: a clapper's knock-knock goes down the empty street, and a voice calls to mind the fire.

spots.name: Hui butchers in the lanes by the mosque
spots.summary: The lanes of the Hui, Chinese-speaking Muslims descended from Central Asian, Persian and Arab settlers, round the Great Mosque: mutton butchers, bread ovens and leather workers.
details: Muslim merchants had lived in Chang'an since the Tang; under the Mongols many more came as soldiers, officials and craftsmen. In Ming Xi'an the Hui community kept its mosques and its halal trades, mutton and beef above all. The paomo soup of bread crumbled into mutton broth is a later Xi'an speciality whose early history is uncertain.

vignettes.text: The call to prayer from the mosque's octagonal pavilion. A butcher in a white cap sharpens his knife; the first sheep are led in from the west gate.
Smoke and the smell of mutton broth fill the lane. A baker slaps flatbreads on the side of a clay oven, as his Tang predecessors did.
After the evening prayer, old men sit outside the mosque gate on low stools and talk of the caravans from Hami.

spots.name: Farmers on the Daming Palace mounds
spots.summary: Villagers ploughing wheat on the Longshou plateau over the Daming Palace, among the earth mounds of its halls and gates.
details: After 904 the palace was never rebuilt. Its rammed-earth terraces stood as mounds, cut into for building earth; the Taiye pond silted into a marsh. Farmers found tiles, bricks and gilded fragments in their fields. Systematic excavation began only in the 1950s.

vignettes.text: A farmer and his ox plough round the foot of a great earth mound, the ploughshare turning up green-glazed roof tiles.
The family eats noodles in the shade of the mound. Children dig a cave in its side to keep the wheat dry.
From the top of the mound the walls and the Bell Tower of Xi'an show grey in the evening haze to the south-west.

events.title: Daxing is founded
events.text: Emperor Wen of Sui decided in 582 to leave the cramped, brackish Han city and build anew to the south-east. Yuwen Kai planned the grid and Gao Jiong led the works: within nine months the walls, palace and offices were ready, and the court moved in during the third month of 583. The city was named after the emperor's old title, Duke of Daxing.

events.title: The Xuanwu Gate incident
events.text: At the north gate of the Palace City, Li Shimin ambushed and killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, who were riding to court. Within days his father Gaozu named him crown prince, and within two months abdicated: Li Shimin reigned as Taizong, the most admired emperor of the dynasty.

events.title: Xuanzang returns from India
events.text: Sixteen years after he left illegally for India, the monk Xuanzang came back with 657 Sanskrit texts, relics and images on some twenty horses. The city turned out: the treasures were paraded along Zhuque Avenue to the Hongfu temple, with crowds so dense, his biography says, that people could not move and incense smoke hung over the street.

events.title: Xuanzang's pagoda is built
events.text: To keep the sutras and relics safe from fire, Xuanzang asked for a stone pagoda; the emperor Gaozong gave a brick one instead, on a high square base in the west court of the Ci'en temple. The biography says the master himself carried bricks. The pagoda soon decayed and was rebuilt under Empress Wu in 701-704.

events.title: The court moves to the Daming Palace
events.text: Gaozong, who suffered in the damp, low Palace City, rebuilt Taizong's abandoned summer palace on the Longshou plateau in 662-663, paid for partly by docking a month of the officials' salaries. In the fourth month of 663 he moved in, and the Daming Palace with its Hanyuan Hall became the seat of the court for the rest of the dynasty.

events.title: Lantern festival: the curfew is lifted
events.text: For three nights of the Lantern Festival the curfew was suspended and the ward gates stood open. In 713 a lantern wheel some 60 m high, hung with brocade and 50,000 lamps, was set up outside the Anfu gate, and over a thousand palace women and young women of the city danced and sang beneath it, the chroniclers say.

events.title: The Emperor's Birthday festival
events.text: From 729 Xuanzong's birthday was a national holiday, the Qianqiu ('Thousand Autumns') festival. At the Xingqing Palace the emperor feasted the court from his tower over the avenue while acrobats, musicians and a hundred dancing horses performed, the horses bowing in time to the music and holding cups of wine in their teeth.

events.title: An Lushan's rebels take Chang'an
events.text: After the Tongguan pass fell, Xuanzong fled at dawn with Yang Guifei and a few guards; at Mawei the soldiers killed her cousin, the chief minister, and forced the emperor to have her strangled. The rebels looted the palaces and the city for over a year until Tang and Uighur troops retook it in late 757.

events.title: The Nestorian stele is set up
events.text: The monk Adam (Jingjing) composed, and a Christian official named Yisi paid for, a 2.8 m stone stele 'commemorating the propagation of the luminous teaching of Da Qin in the Middle Kingdom', with Chinese text, Syriac names and a cross over clouds and a lotus. It was dug up near Xi'an about 1625.

events.title: The Huichang persecution
events.text: Emperor Wuzong, urged by Taoist advisers and short of money, ordered the closure of more than 4,600 monasteries and the return of over 260,000 monks and nuns to lay life; temple bronzes went to the mints. In the capital only four temples were left open. Christians, Zoroastrians and Manichaeans were banned too. The Japanese monk Ennin saw it happen and recorded it.

events.title: Huang Chao enters Chang'an
events.text: The rebel army of the salt smuggler Huang Chao marched in as the emperor Xizong fled to Sichuan. Huang Chao took the throne as emperor of Qi, reportedly in the Hanyuan Hall. When the city resisted, his troops massacred its people; when Tang forces closed in, in 883, they burned much of it as they left.

events.title: Zhu Wen dismantles the capital
events.text: The warlord Zhu Wen forced the emperor Zhaozong to move to Luoyang and had the palaces, offices and houses of Chang'an pulled down; their beams were floated down the Wei and the Yellow River. The people were driven east with the court. The governor Han Jian then walled a small town inside the old Imperial City, the core of later Xi'an.

events.title: The Ming walls are raised
events.text: After taking Shaanxi in 1369 the Ming renamed the city Xi'an, 'Western Peace', and made it the seat of the Prince of Qin and a great frontier garrison. The governors enlarged the old walls of the Imperial City north and east into a rectangle of nearly 14 km, rammed in earth 12 m high, with gates, barbicans, corner towers and a moat.

events.title: The Bell Tower is built
events.text: A bell tower was built near Guangji Street, then the centre of the city, to ring the dawn and the hours; legend says it was raised to calm the earthquakes of the dragon under the city. In 1582 it was taken down and rebuilt a few hundred metres to the east, at the new crossing of the four main streets, where it still stands.

stories.title: A day in the capital of a million
stories.summary: From the dawn drums to the dusk drums in Xuanzong's Chang'an: the government quarter, the West Market and its foreign taverns, a church, a pagoda, and the inns of Pingkang.

steps.title: The dawn drums
steps.text: The drums on the avenues answer the palace drum, and the gates of the 108 wards open one by one. Officials ride out by lantern light to the dawn audience.

steps.title: Zhuque Gate
steps.text: At the head of the 150 m avenue, clerks stream into the Imperial City's ministries. No house opens on the avenue: only ward walls, locust trees and ditches.

steps.title: The West Market
steps.text: The noon drum opens the market. In the lanes: horses, jade, glass, pepper and silver from the West, and Sogdian traders in tall hats calling prices in three languages.

steps.title: A foreign wine shop
steps.text: East of the market a Sogdian woman pours grape wine in amber cups and a dancer whirls on her little rug. Young gallants tie their white horses at the door.

steps.title: The Da Qin monastery
steps.text: In the Yining ward, a Chinese temple whose priests read Syriac: the Christian monastery founded in 638, renamed in 745 'of Da Qin'.

steps.title: The Lesser Wild Goose Pagoda
steps.text: Fifteen storeys of brick rising over the Anren ward, where the monk Yijing translated the texts he brought back from India by sea.

steps.title: Pingkang at dusk
steps.text: The dusk drums beat 800 times and the ward gates close. In Pingkang the candidates' lamps are lit, and so are the courtesans' lanterns.

stories.title: Xuanzang's sutras
stories.summary: Follow the books the pilgrim Xuanzang brought back from India in 645, from the crowds of Zhuque Avenue to the brick pagoda built to keep them.

steps.title: The welcome
steps.text: In 645 the city lines Zhuque Avenue to see 657 Sanskrit books, relics and gold and sandalwood images carried past on some twenty horses.

steps.title: The emperor's preface
steps.text: Taizong, who had wanted to make the monk an official, wrote a preface to his translations in 648, the 'Preface to the Holy Teaching', later carved in stone.

steps.title: The translation court
steps.text: At the new Ci'en temple Xuanzang reads the Sanskrit aloud; a dozen monks check, write and polish the Chinese. He will translate 1,335 scrolls in nineteen years.

steps.title: The pagoda
steps.text: In 652 a brick pagoda rises in the temple's west court to keep the books safe from fire. The master, the story goes, carried bricks himself.

steps.title: Ximing temple
steps.text: In 658 he moves to the new Ximing temple, built by Gaozong, and later to the Yuhua palace in the hills, where he dies in 664.
